entries.summary: This is our comprehensive list of every e-reader we recommend that is available on Amazon. We have products from the Kindle, Kobo, BOOX, Viwoods, Remarkable, Pocketbook, and many more. The post The big list of e-readers you can buy on Amazon in 2026 first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
There are hundreds of E-Readers you can purchase on Amazon, and it’s sometimes hard to know what models are best. There are brands such as the Kindle, Kobo, Pocketbook, Remarkable Meebook, iFlytek, and tons of others. This is the most comprehensive list of the best e-readers you can purchase on Amazon, and this list will be updated regularly, as new devices come out.

entries.title: How to Recover Deleted E-Reader File Formats (Including EPUB and PDF)
entries.summary: It's easy to accidentally delete an important e-book while organizing files or freeing up storage space. Often people don't realize they still need the file until it's already gone. The post How to Recover Deleted E-Reader File Formats (Including EPUB and PDF) first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
It’s easy to accidentally delete an important e-book while organizing files or freeing up storage space. Often people don’t realize they still need the file until it’s already gone. Then they struggle to find any possible way to get it back. In this article, you’ll learn several effective ways to recover deleted e-reader files, including EPUB and PDF.

Which E-Reader File Recovery Method Should You Try?

You don’t need to try every possible method to recover ebook files. Instead, first identify which situation best matches yours. This will help you determine where to start and choose the recovery method most likely to work. Here’s how to do it.

Situation Best recovery method
File was recently deleted on your computer Check Recycle Bin or Trash
You have built-in backups or cloud storage enabled Restore from them
No backup is available Use data recovery software
The book was purchased online Re-download it from your account
The book is synced with your e-reader account Download it again from your cloud library

Methods to Recover Deleted E-Reader Files

We analyzed the most common recovery scenarios discussed in the data recovery community and compiled our own list of the most effective and reliable ones. Below, you’ll find detailed, step-by-step instructions for each recovery method. However, if you don’t have any backups, permanently deleted the file, or deleted it directly on your e-reader, skip straight to the guide on PDF recovery and EPUB recovery using software. Acting quickly gives you the best chance of recovering your e-book before the deleted data is overwritten.

Method 1. Check the Recycle Bin or Trash

When you delete an EPUB, PDF, or another e-book file from your computer, it is usually not erased immediately. On Windows, it may be moved to the Recycle Bin, while on macOS, it may remain in the Trash. This is the easiest place to check first.

To restore deleted EPUB and PDF:

  • Open the Recycle Bin (Win) from the desktop. Or open the Trash (Mac) from the Dock.
  • Look through the deleted files or use the search bar to find the e-book by its name or file extension.
  • Right-click (or double-click) the EPUB, PDF, or other file you want to recover.
  • Select Restore (Win) or Put Back (Mac). The file will return to its original location.

This method won’t work if you have already emptied the Recycle Bin or Trash or permanently deleted the file using a keyboard shortcut, such as Shift + Delete on Windows or Option + Command + Delete on macOS.

Method 2. Restore the File From a Backup

If you regularly back up your computer or set up automatic local/cloud backups before files were deleted, an earlier copy of the deleted e-book may still be available. Windows users can check File History or Previous Versions, while Mac users can restore files through Time Machine.

Option 1. Recover EPUB Files or PDF With File History/Previous Versions

Restore files with File History on Windows:

  • Connect the external drive that contains your File History backup.
  • Open Control Panel.
  • Go to System and Security > File History.
  • Click Restore personal files.
  • Browse to the folder where the deleted files were originally located.
  • Use the arrows to browse available backup versions.
  • Select the files or folders you want to restore.
  • Click the green Restore button.

File History offers another way to recover files directly from the folder where they were originally stored. You can restore a folder to an earlier point in time when it still contained the deleted files.

Restore files using Previous Versions on Windows:

  • Open the folder that originally contained the deleted files.
  • Right-click an empty area inside the folder and select Properties.
  • Open the Previous Versions tab.
  • Select the version created before the files were deleted.
  • Click Open to verify that it contains the files you want to recover.
  • Click Restore to return the folder to that version, or choose Restore To if you’d rather save it to a different location.

Option 2. Recover EPUB Files or PDF With Time Machine

Restore files using Time Machine on macOS:

  • Connect your Time Machine backup drive.
  • Open the folder where the e-book was originally stored.
  • Click the Time Machine icon in the menu bar and select Browse Time Machine Backups.
  • Use the timeline on the right side of the screen or the arrows to browse through older backups until you find the date when the photos were still available.
  • Select the missing EPUB, PDF, or other e-book file.
  • Click Restore. Time Machine will return the file to its original folder.

Option 3. Check a Cloud Backup

If you use OneDrive, Google Drive, iCloud Drive, or another cloud service:

  • Sign in to your cloud storage account.
  • Open the folder where the e-book was stored.
  • Check whether the file is still available.
  • If it is missing, open the service’s Trash, Recycle Bin, or Recently Deleted section.
  • Select the file.
  • Click Restore.

Method 3. Recover Files With Recovery Software

Data recovery software scans your storage device for deleted files that are no longer accessible through the operating system. It can recover EPUB, PDF, and many other e-book formats while preserving their original filenames and folder structure.

We understand that many people have never used data recovery software before or may not have advanced technical skills. That’s why we’ll use Disk Drill Data Recovery as an example. It has a simple, intuitive interface that’s easy to navigate, even for beginners, and at the same time delivers excellent PDF and EPUB file recovery performance. This is a completely safe tool reviewed by many users. The software is available for both Windows and macOS, includes a preview feature so you can check files before recovering them, and displays each file’s recovery chances. On Windows, you can recover up to 100 MB of data for free. On macOS, you can scan storage devices and preview recoverable files for free with no limits.

Recover deleted EPUB files/PDF with Disk Drill:

  • Download and install Disk Drill.
  • Connect the storage device to your computer.
  • Launch Disk Drill.
  • Select the drive where the deleted file was stored.
  • Click Search for lost data. If prompted, use Universal Scan.
  • Wait for the scan to finish, then click Review found items to browse the results.
  • Use the Preview feature to verify files before recovery. You can use the search bar or file filters to find the missing e-book. Search by the file name or enter an extension such as: .epub; .pdf; .mobi; .azw3; .fb2; .cbz; .cbr
  • Select the files you want to restore.
  • Click Recover.
  • Choose a destination on your computer, an external drive, or another storage device. And click Next.

Note: If the file was deleted directly from the e-reader and you cannot re-download it or restore it from cloud storage, try connecting the device to your computer and scanning it with data recovery software. This is only possible if the e-reader supports the USB Mass Storage Class (MSC) protocol, which allows the computer to recognize it as a removable drive, similar to a USB flash drive. Most older e-readers support MSC, while many newer models use the Media Transfer Protocol (MTP) instead. Devices that connect only through MTP cannot be scanned directly by data recovery software.

Method 4. Re-download the E-Book

If you purchased or downloaded the e-book from an online store, you may be able to download it again. Platforms such as Kindle, Kobo, Google Play Books, and Apple Books usually keep purchased titles linked to your account.

Re-download a purchased e-book:

  • Open the website or application where you purchased the book.
  • Sign in with the same account you used for the original purchase.
  • Open your Library, Purchased Books, or My Books section.
  • Find the missing title.
  • Select Download, Read, or Send to Device.
  • Choose your computer, phone, tablet, or e-reader as the destination.

For books from free sources such as Project Gutenberg, search for the title again and download a new copy in EPUB, PDF, or another available format.

Method 5. Check Your E-Reader’s Cloud Library

Many e-readers automatically synchronize purchased books with an online account. Deleting a book from the device may remove only the downloaded copy, while the title remains available in the cloud library.

Restore a book from the cloud library:

  • Sign in to the account connected to the device.
  • Open the device’s Library.
  • Switch from downloaded books to All, Cloud, or a similar view.
  • Find the missing title.
  • Tap the book or select the download icon.
  • Wait for the book to download again.

Depending on the service, your bookmarks, notes, highlights, and reading progress may also be restored through synchronization.

Conclusion

Before you give up on a missing e-book, take a few minutes to identify how it was lost. In many cases, recently deleted EPUB and PDF files can be restored from the Recycle Bin, Trash, a backup, or your e-reader’s cloud library. If none of those options are available, data recovery software will help recover deleted PDF files or EPUB that haven’t been overwritten.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I recover deleted EPUB files after emptying the Recycle Bin or Trash?

Yes. If local or cloud backups were enabled before the file was deleted, you may be able to restore it from there. If no backup is available, your best option is to use data recovery software, provided the deleted data hasn’t been overwritten.

Which e-book file formats can be recovered?

Most data recovery software supports many popular e-book formats, including EPUB, PDF, MOBI, AZW3, FB2, CBZ, and CBR.

Can I recover only specific e-books instead of restoring everything?

Yes. Disk Drill lets you preview files, and recover only the e-books you need instead of restoring everything found during the scan.

entries.title: E-Ink Gaming Guide: Can You Play Web-Based Games and Slots on Modern Color E-Paper Tablets?
entries.summary: So, can you play web-based games and slots on a modern colour e-paper tablet? The answer is a definitive yes, provided you choose the right hardware. The post E-Ink Gaming Guide: Can You Play Web-Based Games and Slots on Modern Color E-Paper Tablets? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
We’ve all seen how far e-readers have come over the last decade. Gone are the days when these devices were strictly reserved for reading monochrome novels in direct sunlight. With recent technological leaps, colour e-paper has made massive strides, leaving many of us wondering if these low-power, eye-friendly screens can handle anything beyond digital novels and daily newspapers. Can you actually use them to play casual web-based games or spin online slots?

To figure out if modern colour tablets are up to the task, we have to look closely at the two competing screen technologies dominating the market today: E Ink Kaleido 3 and E Ink Gallery 3. They take fundamentally different approaches to displaying colour, and the differences in their hardware capabilities are vast.

Kaleido 3 is currently the most popular choice for modern colour e-paper tablets. It works by layering a Colour Filter Array (CFA) directly over a standard black-and-white Carta 1200 e-paper display. This filter scatters red, green, and blue light, allowing the screen to display up to 4,096 colours. Because it relies on a standard monochrome layer underneath, the screen remains incredibly responsive. The main trade-off is that colour resolution drops to 150 pixels per inch (ppi), whilst black-and-white text stays at a razor-sharp 300 ppi. The colours can also look slightly muted, almost like a faded Sunday newspaper layout.

On the other hand, we have Gallery 3, which uses an entirely different design known as Advanced Color ePaper (ACeP). Instead of a colour filter, Gallery 3 uses four distinct coloured pigments (cyan, magenta, yellow, and white) within each individual microcapsule. This allows for rich, fully saturated colours at a pin-sharp 300 ppi. It looks brilliant, but there’s a major catch. Moving those four physical pigments around inside the screen takes a long time. Whilst a Kaleido 3 screen can refresh in a fraction of a second, Gallery 3 can take up to a second or more just to render a single page update. If you try to run any kind of animation, Gallery 3 becomes painfully sluggish. For casual gaming and browser-based slots, Kaleido 3 is currently the only viable option.

Software, Refresh Rates, and Onyx Boox Super Refresh (BSR)

Of course, hardware is only half the battle. Even with a responsive screen like Kaleido 3, standard e-paper is naturally prone to lagging. That’s where clever software and custom hardware controllers come into play. Modern e-paper tablets, particularly those from Onyx Boox, run on full versions of the Android operating system, giving you access to standard web browsers like Chrome and Firefox.

But how do they overcome the sluggishness inherent in physical ink microcapsules? The answer lies in proprietary refresh technology, most notably Onyx Boox Super Refresh (BSR). This is a dedicated graphics coprocessor integrated into the tablet’s motherboard, designed solely to speed up screen updates and manage ghosting.

Instead of relying on the slow, traditional full-screen flash that we associate with older e-readers, BSR offers custom refresh modes tailored to different tasks:

  • HD Mode: Designed for reading static text, offering the sharpest detail with minimal ghosting, but at a very slow refresh rate.
  • Balanced Mode: Great for typing or scrolling through simple documents, balancing text clarity with faster transitions.
  • Fast Mode: Optimised for browsing web pages, allowing smooth scrolling whilst sacrificing a bit of image quality.
  • Ultrafast Mode: This mode pushes the screen to its absolute physical limits, dropping the image resolution slightly to achieve frame rates that can actually display video and casual motion.

By choosing Ultrafast mode, the screen keeps up with moving objects by refreshing individual pixels dynamically rather than waiting to refresh the entire display. Many of us have experienced the annoyance of slow screen updates on older e-readers; BSR largely solves this. Yes, you will notice some ghosting (faint shadows of previous images remaining on the screen), but the latency drops low enough that interactive web pages actually become usable. It’s a brilliant bit of engineering that turns a passive e-reader into an interactive tablet.

Web Browser Performance: Evaluating HTML5 Rendering and Frame Rates

So, how does all this technology translate to the web browser? If you open a browser like Google Chrome or the e-ink optimised EinkBro on a modern Kaleido 3 tablet, you will find that standard HTML5 pages render surprisingly well.

Modern web-based games, casual puzzles, and online slots are built using HTML5 and JavaScript, which means they run directly within the browser without needing heavy external plugins. When you load one of these platforms on a colour e-paper tablet, the device has to render complex graphical layouts, CSS animations, and real-time script updates.

The processing power of the octa-core Snapdragon chips found in modern e-paper tablets handles the underlying code easily. The real bottleneck is the frame rate of the screen. Whilst a standard smartphone or iPad runs at a silky smooth 60Hz or 120Hz, an e-paper screen on Ultrafast mode generally hovers around 12 to 15 frames per second.

For fast-paced action games, this frame rate is admittedly too low. However, for casual web-based games, turn-based puzzles, card games, and online slots, 15 frames per second is surprisingly playable. The main visual challenge is screen ghosting. As graphical elements move across the screen, they leave behind light trails. To combat this, most modern tablets allow you to trigger a manual full-screen refresh with a quick tap of a navigation button, instantly clearing any visual clutter and keeping the display looking clean.

Real-World Casual Gaming Test: Rainbow Riches on E-Paper

To see how these theories hold up in practice, we decided to run a real-world test. We loaded up the browser on an Onyx Boox tablet featuring a Kaleido 3 display, navigated to Virgin Games, and opened the classic HTML5 slot, rainbow riches .

This particular game is an excellent benchmark for this hardware. It features a bright Irish countryside theme filled with vibrant green hills, gold coins, and colourful rainbow paths. In addition to the detailed artwork, the spinning reels provide a rigorous test for screen latency and ghosting.

We set the tablet to Ultrafast mode and loaded the game. The first thing we noticed was the colour palette. Whilst the greens and golds weren’t as neon or intense as they would be on an OLED screen, they looked incredibly pleasing and organic, almost like looking at a beautifully printed board game manual.

When we hit the spin button, the physical ink particles went to work. During the rapid rotation of the reels, the symbols naturally blurred, and a bit of ghosting was visible. However, thanks to the BSR technology, the motion was continuous rather than choppy. As soon as the reels stopped spinning, the screen settled quickly, and the static icons became perfectly sharp again. For a casual gaming session, the experience was remarkably comfortable and fully functional. It proved that modern colour e-paper can handle the quick visual updates of a classic online slot without compromising the overall enjoyment of the game.

Wellbeing Benefits: Eye Comfort and Battery Efficiency

Given that standard tablets offer superior frame rates and richer colours, you might wonder why anyone would choose to play on an e-paper device in the first place. The answer comes down to two major benefits: eye health and battery efficiency.

Standard tablets use emissive LCD or OLED screens, which means they blast bright light, including high levels of blue light, directly into your eyes. Spending hours staring at these screens, especially in low-light environments, can lead to digital eye strain, dry eyes, and disrupted sleep patterns. E-paper, on the other hand, is a reflective display. It works exactly like real paper, reflecting the ambient light in the room. Even when you use the built-in front light on an e-paper tablet, the LEDs are positioned around the bezel, shining down onto the screen rather than straight out at your face. I find that this creates a much more relaxing experience, allowing you to enjoy a casual game in the evening without feeling wired afterwards.

Then there is the battery efficiency. Standard tablets are notorious battery hogs, usually needing a charge every day or two, especially if you are running interactive web applications. Whilst utilising high-frequency refresh modes like BSR does drain more battery than simply reading a static EPUB, e-paper tablets still consume a fraction of the power required by a bright LCD panel. You can easily get several days of mixed-use out of a single charge, making these devices excellent companions for long journeys where power outlets might be scarce.

Of course, if you do decide to play casual web-based slots or other games on your device, it’s important to keep things balanced. Always ensure you are playing responsibly, setting personal limits on your time and spend, and keeping it as a light form of entertainment. In the UK, organisations like BeGambleAware offer excellent free support and resources (always ensure you are over 18 before playing).

A New Way to Play

So, can you play web-based games and slots on a modern colour e-paper tablet? The answer is a definitive yes, provided you choose the right hardware. Whilst a Gallery 3 screen will leave you frustrated by its slow update times, a Kaleido 3 tablet equipped with a dedicated graphics accelerator like Onyx’s BSR technology handles casual, browser-based games surprisingly well.

You will have to accept some compromises, including slightly softer colours and a bit of screen ghosting during rapid animations. But if you value a display that is exceptionally gentle on your eyes, performs brilliantly in direct sunlight, and boasts a battery life that standard tablets can only dream of, colour e-paper offers a genuinely compelling alternative for your casual downtime.

Markus lives in San Francisco, California and is the video game and audio expert on Good e-Reader! He has a huge interest in new e-readers and tablets, and gaming.

entries.title: New Study looks at Canadian E-book Reading Habits
entries.summary: Ebooks are an integral part of the Canadian book market. Nearly 14% of all books purchased by Canadians in 2025 were ebooks, according to the Canadian Book Consumer Study 2025. At the same time, 71% of Canadians reported reading an ebook in 2025. The post New Study looks at Canadian E-book Reading Habits first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Ebooks have become a key player in the Canadian book market. The Canadian Book Consumer Study 2025 indicates that in 2025, ebooks accounted for nearly 14% of all book purchases by Canadians. Furthermore, the Canadian Leisure & Reading Study 2025 revealed that a significant 71% of Canadians chose to read an ebook that year.

In terms of borrowers, “29% of all Canadian book borrowers borrowed ebooks” in 2025, with “half of all books borrowed from the library” by “ebook borrowers” in 2025 being ebooks (50%), followed by print (32%) and audio (18%). Overall, 17% of books borrowed by Canadians book borrowers were ebooks, compared to print (74%) and audio (9%).

The study also found that fiction dominated among Canadian ebook readers: 71% of purchases were fiction, and 29% nonfiction.

Within those purchases, romance led the way among fiction purchases for ebook readers, accounting for 19% of ebook purchases vs. 10% of all book purchases; followed by thrillers, (16% of ebook purchases vs. 16% of all book purchases); fantasy (13% of ebook purchases vs. 17% of all purchases); and mysteries (13% of ebook purchases, also level with other format purchases).

The most popular nonfiction subjects were self-help (21% of ebook purchases vs. 19% of all purchases); history (16% of ebook purchases vs. 13% of all purchases) and biography and memoir (15% of ebook purchases vs. 20% of all purchases).

Highlights

  • 71% of Canadians read an ebook in 2025.
  • 34% of all Canadian book buyers bought ebooks and 29% of all Canadian book borrowers borrowed ebooks last year. Canadian ebook buyers spent an average of $11.85 per ebook in 2025.
  • 56% of ebook buyers reported receiving excellent value for money from their ebook purchases.
  • Ebook buyers were more influenced by price than all buyers: 41% of Canadian ebook buyers purchased their books at a specific location due to a good price, offer, or promo compared with only 29% of Canadian book buyers.
  • Ebook buyers were more likely to buy the book for themselves rather than someone else (96%) than all book buyers (84%).
  • 48% of Canadian ebook borrowers visited the library to pick up holds.
  • 55% of Canadian ebook borrowers gave wanting to save money as the reason they borrowed rather than bought their ebooks.
  • 54% of ebook borrowers searched for books by Canadian authors/illustrators. A higher share than all borrowers (52%), ebook purchasers (44%), or all buyers (38%).
  • Over half of all Canadian ebook readers in 2025 read between one and five ebooks last year (59%).
  • 81% of Canadian ebook readers agreed or sometimes agreed that they get good value for ebooks at the price they pay.
  • The largest share of ebook readers used their smartphones to read their books (36%).

via Booknet Canada

entries.title: Rakuten Kobo e-readers now sold in Best Buy US Stores
entries.summary: Kobo e-readers are officially stocked directly by Best Buy in the United States, featuring popular models like the Clara BW, Clara Color, and Libra Colour available for online shipping and select in-store pickup. The post Rakuten Kobo e-readers now sold in Best Buy US Stores first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Rakuten Kobo has just quietly started doing business in the USA at Best Buy. They are stocking the latest-generation Kobo Libra Colour, Kobo Clara Colour, and the Kobo Clara BW. They are also stocking Kobo Pens, Kobo Remotes, Cases and Gift Cards. The e-readers and accessories are available in stores and online. There are no demo units in the stores yet, as they are in Canada.

Walmart and Rakuten Kobo partnered in 2018 to sell e-readers in over 1,000 US locations and online. As soon as this partnership was established, Walmart launched Walmart ebooks, allowing users who bought an e-reader from Walmart to purchase ebooks through Walmart. There was a dedicated Walmart ebooks app for Android and iOS that made things easier. Right off the bat, things were rocky. Kobo expected a US retail giant to have demo e-readers for people to try before buying. Many locations did not stock e-readers; the ones who did often had dead batteries and were never charged. Nobody was trained on the e-readers, so they couldn’t answer simple questions. They were primarily sold online and sometimes in stores. The partnership was officially dead on October 31st, 2024, and the app was shut down.

This is the first time since 2024 that Kobo has found another retail partner in the USA to sell its e-readers and accessories. They should also be discounted from time to time, as part of Kobo sales. It will be an uphill battle for Kobo, which has never had much market share in the USA. This is because Amazon Kindle e-readers are fully available both online and in physical retail locations across Best Buy USA. They started to sell Kindles back in 2010, and many people buy them from this store.

Hardware

By removing the extra layer of protective cover glass, the device minimizes screen reflections and improves text contrast. The absence of a flush screen and bezel contributes to amazing contrast.

This e-reader is designed for reading books, and users can access the Pocketbook Store to download thousands of books. It offers extensive support for ACSM, AZW, AZW3, CBR, CBZ, CHM, DJVU, DOC, DOCX, EPUB (DRM), EPUB, FB2, FB2.ZIP, HTM, HTML, MOBI, PDF (DRM), PDF, PRC, RTF, and TXT. With DRM EPUB and PDF, users can purchase ebooks from other stores such as Barnes & Noble, Kobo, and Google.

You can use Libby natively on the Era Lite via the built-in PocketBook x Libby app. Introduced in late 2025 via firmware version 6.10 or higher, this official integration allows you to browse, borrow, and read library titles directly on your e-reader without using a computer web browser or transferring files over Adobe Digital Editions. Ebooks can be downloaded for offline reading within the borrowing period.”, according to OverDrive. Downloaded files automatically load inside the native PocketBook Reading app. Borrowed titles return automatically when the loan period expires, but you can choose to return them early directly from your device desktop or the app’s “Manage Loan” interface

Users can also enjoy the convenience of 11 preloaded dictionaries and explore an additional 42 language combinations, available for free download. Whether learning a new language or enhancing your language skills, PocketBook Verse Lite is the perfect companion for language enthusiasts.

Last year, PocketBook launched a UK bookstore, and most of its new e-readers have the store built in, no matter what country they live in. It offers 4.5 million e-books and 90,000 audiobooks that cover every genre. Readers gain access not only to timeless favourites but also to international premieres – with many of the world’s top bestsellers available on the same day as their global release. Regular updates, diverse genres, and works from renowned authors ensure the store remains dynamic, relevant, and full of discoveries.

With a pay-per-download model, UK readers now have direct access to millions of e-books and audiobooks. This expansion highlights PocketBook’s commitment to delivering the most advanced and user-friendly reading experiences worldwide.

“We’re proud to open this new PocketBook chapter in the UK. By adding Gardner’s rich catalog to our ecosystem, we’re making e-reading even more accessible to users across the UK,” said Enrico Mueller, Managing Director of PocketBook Readers GmbH. “We are also glad to offer content, protected by LCP DRM: with this solution, we ensure greater flexibility and fewer barriers – staying true to our mission of making reading as user-friendly as possible.”

“We are delighted to be working with PocketBook to bring our Publishers’ e-books and audiobooks to new heights, giving the UK public full access to the Gardners catalog”, stated Ali Balaban, Gardners’ Head of Digital Product. “As a trusted partner in the book business, we are excited to be working with our first e-reader brand”.

Nigel Wyman, Chief Sales Officer, commented, “This is a culmination of hard work between PocketBook and the Gardners’ team. We are pleased to be able to finally offer our full catalog of digital products to a wider audience in the UK via this collaboration”.

Wrap Up

The PocketBook Era Lite offers a specific set of benefits tailored for readers who want physical buttons, premium screen tech, and freedom from closed e-book ecosystems.

Superior Text Clarity & Contrast

    • Sunken Screen Benefit: By removing the flush glass cover layer, it eliminates a layer of glare.
    • Newer Tech: It uses an E Ink Carta 1300 panel, which provides sharper text and faster page turns than the older standard Era.
    • Less Reflection: The recessed design mimics physical paper better than smooth, glossy screens.
    • Physical Buttons: Side page-turn buttons let you read comfortably with one hand without smudging the screen.
    • Auto-Rotation: A built-in G-sensor automatically flips the orientation, making it equally comfortable for left- and right-handed readers.
    • Remappable Layout: You can fully customize what the four hardware buttons do in the Linux settings.
    • No File Conversion: Natively supports 25 file formats (including EPUB, PDF, AZW, and MOBI).
    • Drag-and-Drop Friendly: You do not need to use proprietary software like Calibre or Amazon Send-to-Kindle to load your books.
    • Multiple Sync Options: Move files easily via Dropbox, Send-to-PocketBook, or a direct USB-C cable.
  • Native Libby App: Unlike Kindles outside the US, the built-in Libby app lets you browse, borrow, and download library books directly on the device over Wi-Fi.
  • Open DRM Support: Built-in Adobe and LCP DRM compatibility means you can buy books from almost any digital store worldwide.

entries.title: Inkleaf is a dual screen e-reader set for a Kickstarter Launch
entries.summary: The InkLeaf device is a dual-screen foldable E Ink notebook that connects two 10.3-inch Carta E Ink panels with a notebook-style hinge, letting users read reference material on one side and write handwritten notes on the other simultaneously. The post Inkleaf is a dual screen e-reader set for a Kickstarter Launch first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Inkleaf foldable digital notebook is a dual-screen E Ink tablet built specifically to solve the “split-screen problem” by allowing you to read a textbook on one side while taking notes on the other. The tablet is built to mimic the physical experience of a hardcover book.

The Inkleaf is a dual-screen E Ink digital notebook engineered with a premium cast aluminum body and a precision hinge barrel that allows it to fold completely flat into a 180-degree, two-page layout. The device features two 10.3-inch E Ink Carta 1300 panels designed to look and feel like an open hardcover book. Despite housing two full-sized screens, it remains remarkably portable, measuring just 4.2mm thin per individual panel (8.4mm when folded closed) and weighing a mere 480 grams.

Under the hood, the hardware runs on a quad-core Cortex-A35 processor, 2 GB RAM, and 64 GB onboard storage. It is powered by a 3,200 mAh battery that delivers up to two weeks of battery life on a single charge. It provides native, format-restriction-free support for PDF, EPUB, MOBI, and TXT files, eliminating recurring subscription fees for managing personal documents. The tablet also features integrated, on-device AI-powered handwriting search that lets users instantly locate phrases across all of their handwritten notebooks, alongside a specialized Secondary Display Mode that allows it to function as an eye-strain-free portable monitor for external devices.

The Inkleaf is going to run on Google Android, but it has not been disclosed on what version it is running or if it will include access to the Google Play Store to download millions of free apps. It would be dire if the company only allowed for the sideloading of apps, which would limit mass market appeal.

For writing and user input, the system includes physical page-navigation buttons and ships with a Wacom-supported, pressure-sensitive stylus that operates without a battery or charging requirements. The pen mimics the drag of a physical pen on paper and supports intuitive gesture controls, such as flipping the pen to erase or using shortcuts to flick open documents from one screen to the other. It will have 4096 levels of pressure sensitivity. Currently priced at approximately $450 USD, the initial founder and crowdfunding hardware batches are scheduled to ship in August 2026, with a broader commercial retail rollout planned for 2027.
